title: Index funds: owning the whole market

sections.body: An index fund buys every company in a market index, such as the S&P 500, which tracks about 500 large US companies. Instead of guessing which stocks will win, you own a small slice of all of them.

items: Diversification: one company failing has only a small effect on you.
Low cost: no team of stock pickers to pay, so yearly fees can be tiny.
Simple: you don't need to research or trade individual stocks.

sections.body: Fees matter. On $100,000, a 0.03% fee costs about $30 a year. A 1% fee costs $1,000 a year, and that gap compounds over decades.
Over long periods, most actively managed funds have trailed their index after fees. That's a big reason many investors choose low-cost index funds for the core of their portfolio.
Index funds still go up and down with the market. They're built for long-term money you won't need for years, not for your emergency fund.

quiz.q: What does an index fund do?
options: Picks a few stocks it thinks will win
Buys all the companies in an index
quiz.why: It tracks an index by owning the companies in it.

quiz.q: On $100,000, how much does a 1% yearly fee cost?
Can an index fund lose value?
options: Yes, it moves with the market
Only if the fund company closes
quiz.why: Diversification lowers single-company risk, but the whole market can still fall.
